title: A new perspective on the anomalous Hall effect
authors: Jason G. Kattan, Matthew Albert, J. E. Sipe
abstract: We revisit the anomalous Hall effect in magnetic conductors, and its generalization to finite frequencies, using a formalism based on microscopic notions of polarization, magnetization, and free charges and currents. The electronic degrees of freedom are treated within second-quantized field theory, where the Hamiltonian features a static and cell-periodic magnetic field that encodes the magnetic order in the crystal and breaks time-reversal symmetry. We study the dynamics of bound and free charge carriers at the microscopic level as they respond to a spatially uniform electric field at finite frequency. The conductivity tensor describing the long-wavelength response is a sum of three terms, including a Kubo term associated with the polarization response, along with the metallic Drude term and the anomalous Hall conductivity that are associated with the longitudinal and transverse parts of the free current response, respectively. We also present numerical calculations of these contributions for the ferromagnetic body-centered cubic phase of iron.
summary: This theoretical work develops a microscopic formalism to analyze the anomalous Hall effect and general optical response in magnetic conductors at finite frequencies. By treating electronic degrees of freedom via second-quantized field theory, the authors decompose the conductivity tensor into three physically distinct parts: polarization (Kubo), Drude, and anomalous Hall contributions. This provides a unified dynamic picture for charge transport beyond static DC measurements.
main_problem: The paper revisits the anomalous Hall effect (AHE) in magnetic conductors, generalizing its study to finite frequencies using a microscopic formalism.
main_result: The long-wavelength conductivity tensor is shown to be a sum of three distinct contributions: a Kubo term from polarization response, and two terms (Drude and anomalous Hall) from the free current response.
method: The analysis employs second-quantized field theory, decomposing charge/current into microscopic polarization, magnetization, and free components derived via lattice gauge theory concepts.
model_or_system: The system is magnetic conductors with long-range magnetic order, modeled using an electronic Hamiltonian incorporating a static, cell-periodic magnetic field that breaks time-reversal symmetry. Calculations are performed for the bcc phase of iron.
key_observables: Long-wavelength conductivity tensor $\sigma(\omega)$, polarization ($\mathbf{P}$), magnetization ($\mathbf{M}$), and free charge/current densities ($ho_F, \mathbf{j}_F$).
important_parameters: Finite frequency ($\omega$), magnetic field strength (encoded in the Hamiltonian), and characteristic length scales ($\Delta$ for spatial averaging).
main_assumptions: The analysis uses a frozen-ion approximation ($\Gamma$ fixed) and relies on long-wavelength approximations.
figures_summary: Not specified by notes, but calculations are presented for iron's bcc phase showing frequency dependence of conductivity contributions.
paper_structure: The paper builds the formalism by defining microscopic quantities (polarization, magnetization) and then derives the macroscopic response ($\sigma(\omega)$) by combining three distinct theoretical terms: Kubo, Drude, and anomalous Hall components.
why_interesting: While focused on condensed matter transport, the decomposition of conductivity into fundamental responses (polarization vs. free current) provides a rigorous framework for understanding linear response in magnetically ordered systems, which has parallels to open quantum system descriptions.
